subject: chemistry
question_text: Balance the following redox reaction by the ion-electron method (in acidic medium): MnO₄⁻(aq) + SO₂(g) → Mn²⁺(aq) + HSO₄⁻(aq).

verification.note: Chapter 5 (Stoichiometry) is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.66-72), which prints the question, its star rank, the citation [March-09] and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. This chapter has NO Long Answer section in the book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The final equation was independently re-checked: atoms Mn 2=2, S 5=5, O 20=20, H 5=5; charge −1 on each side.

steps.label: Identifying the two half reactions
lines: S in SO₂ is +4 → +6 in HSO₄⁻ : oxidation
Mn in MnO₄⁻ is +7 → +2 in Mn²⁺ : reduction
steps.why: The oxidation numbers identify the halves: sulphur rises two units, manganese falls five, which later sets the multipliers 5 and 2.
common_mistakes: Computing S in HSO₄⁻ as +4. With one H at +1, four O at −2 and charge −1, sulphur is +6.
Mislabelling the halves — permanganate is the oxidising agent, so it is reduced.
steps.memory_tip: Write the oxidation number over the changing atom in all four species before splitting the halves.
steps.margin_note: Both skeleton halves with the +4→+6 and +7→+2 changes earn this mark.

steps.label: Balanced oxidation half
lines: Balance O with H₂O, H with H⁺, charge with e⁻:
steps.why: Two water molecules supply the two extra oxygens; of their four hydrogens one stays inside HSO₄⁻ and three leave as H⁺, and the charge check fixes two electrons.
common_mistakes: Writing 4H⁺ and forgetting the hydrogen kept inside HSO₄⁻.
Using one H₂O instead of two.
steps.memory_tip: HSO₄⁻ keeps one hydrogen for itself — only three of the four go out as H⁺.
steps.margin_note: Equation (1) with its charge check earns this mark.

steps.label: Balanced reduction half
steps.why: The permanganate half in acid is the standard five-electron reduction, confirmed by the charge check.
common_mistakes: Writing 3e⁻ or 7e⁻ without the charge check.
Putting the 8H⁺ on the product side.
steps.memory_tip: Permanganate to Mn²⁺ in acid: 8H⁺ in, 4H₂O out, 5e⁻ gained — the same line in every acid-medium permanganate question.
steps.margin_note: Equation (2) with its charge check earns this mark.

steps.label: Adding and the final equation
lines: Add and cancel 15H⁺ and 8H₂O from both sides:
Check: Mn 2=2, S 5=5, O 20=20, H 5=5; charge −1 = −1
steps.why: After equalising at ten electrons, 15 of the 16 H⁺ cancel and 8 of the 10 H₂O cancel, leaving the unusual but correct single H⁺ and 2H₂O on the reactant side.
common_mistakes: Cancelling the H⁺ completely. Exactly one H⁺ survives on the left.
Cancelling all the water. Two H₂O survive on the left.
Skipping the final atom-and-charge check, which is what catches both slips.
steps.memory_tip: The final line keeps one H⁺ and two H₂O — reaching exactly these numbers means the cancellation was done right.
steps.margin_note: The boxed equation with the atom and charge check earns this mark.

insider_note: Asked in March 2009. The lone H⁺ in the final equation looks wrong and tempts students to 'fix' it — the atom and charge check on the last line is what confirms the answer.
